title: Earth's Spin & Orbit
keyIdea: Earth moves in two ways at once. It spins on its axis, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, once about every 24 hours. The half facing the Sun has day and the other half has night, and the spin makes the Sun seem to rise in the east and set in the west. Earth also orbits the Sun, travelling all the way round it once about every 365 days. That trip is one year, and Earth spins about 365 times on the way.
familyTip: In a dark room, shine a torch at a ball and stick a small sticker on it for your home. Turn the ball slowly anticlockwise and say when the sticker reaches sunrise, midday, sunset and midnight. Then walk the spinning ball in a big circle round the torch and count the turns: that is a year of days.

kid: Earth moves in two ways at the same time. It spins, like a top. Think of a line through Earth from the North Pole to the South Pole. That line is the axis. Earth spins round it once in about 24 hours. That is one day.

The Sun can only light up the half of Earth that faces it. That half has day. The other half is in the dark, so it has night. As Earth turns, your home goes from the light into the dark and back again.
The Sun does not move across the sky. It only looks that way. Earth turns towards the Sun, so the Sun seems to come up in the east. Later Earth turns away, and the Sun seems to go down in the west.

Earth also travels all the way round the Sun, on a path called an orbit. One trip takes about 365 days. We call that a year. On the way, Earth spins about 365 times, once for each day. Each time your birthday comes round, Earth has gone round the Sun once more.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. This matches Year 5 Earth and space in the National Curriculum in England: describe the movement of the Earth relative to the Sun, and use the idea of Earth's rotation to explain day and night and the apparent movement of the Sun across the sky. Key words: rotate, spin, axis, orbit, revolve, day, year, Sun-facing side, apparent movement, east, west.

Earth rotates anticlockwise when seen from above the North Pole, which is why the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west. Measured from noon to noon, one rotation is 24 hours (against the stars it is about 23 hours 56 minutes). One orbit takes about 365 and a quarter days, so the calendar adds 29 February in most years divisible by 4. The orbit is almost a circle, and the Sun is far bigger than drawn.

Common mistakes: thinking the Sun goes round Earth each day; thinking the Sun goes out, hides behind hills or is covered by the Moon at night; mixing up the spin and the orbit, so that one trip round the Sun makes one day; and thinking it is day everywhere at once. Children may also say Earth spins once a year. Ask them to point to where it is night right now.

In the lab your child spins Earth through 24 hours, finds a time when Ava has night and Ben, on the far side, has day, watches the Sun cross Ava's sky while only Earth turns, carries Earth once round the Sun in 365 days and sorts six events into spin or orbit. The challenge targets each of the mistakes above.

choices: Our side of Earth faces away from the Sun
practice.hint: The Sun is always shining. What has turned?
practice.explain: Earth spins, so our side turns away from the Sun. Then we are in the dark half of Earth, and it is night.

practice.prompt: Earth spins once every 24 hours. How many hours does it take to spin {n} times?
practice.hint: Each spin is 24 hours. Add 24 for each spin, or multiply.
practice.explain: {n} spins × 24 hours = {=24*n} hours. That is {n} days.

practice.prompt: What is one trip of Earth all the way round the Sun called?
practice.hint: How long does it take for your birthday to come back?
practice.explain: One orbit of the Sun takes about 365 days. That is one year.

practice.prompt: Earth goes round the Sun once a year. How many times does it go round in {n} years?
practice.hint: Earth makes one whole trip round the Sun in each year, so count one trip for every year.
practice.explain: One orbit each year, so in {n} years Earth goes round the Sun {n} times.

practice.prompt: The Sun seems to move across the sky from east to west. What is really moving?
practice.hint: In the lab, which one did you turn?
practice.explain: Earth spins. The Sun stays still, but as we turn, it seems to move across our sky.

pool.hint: Earth spins round it, like a top spins round its middle.
pool.explain: The axis is an imaginary line through the poles. Earth spins round it.

pool.prompt: It is midday where you live. What is it on the far side of Earth?
pool.hint: Which half of Earth is facing the Sun?
pool.explain: Your half faces the Sun, so the far half faces away. It is night there.

pool.prompt: How long does one spin of Earth take?
pool.hint: One spin gives one day and one night.
pool.explain: Earth spins once in about 24 hours. That is one day.

pool.prompt: It is {h} am for Ava. Earth spins on for 3 more hours. What time is it for Ava now (am)?
pool.hint: Each hour of spin moves Ava's clock on 1 hour.

pool.prompt: How long does Earth take to go once round the Sun?
pool.hint: Think of the time from one birthday to the next.
pool.explain: One orbit takes about 365 days, which is one year.

pool.prompt: In which direction does the Sun seem to rise?
pool.hint: The Sun seems to rise on one side and set on the other.
pool.explain: As Earth spins, the Sun seems to rise in the east and set in the west.

pool.prompt: Sam is {a} years old. How many times has Earth gone round the Sun since Sam was born?
pool.hint: Each year of Sam's life, Earth made one whole trip round the Sun. Count one trip per year.
pool.explain: One trip round the Sun each year, so {a} times.

pool.prompt: Which one is a spin, not an orbit?
pool.hint: Which one takes about a day?
pool.explain: Day turning into night happens as Earth spins. The others take a whole year, one orbit.

pool.prompt: Leo says the Sun goes round Earth every day. What is right?
choices: Earth spins, so the Sun only seems to move
The Sun goes round once a year
pool.explain: Earth spins once a day. The Sun stays put and only seems to cross the sky.
